risks.title: Unverified ICE roundup rumors causing panic
risks.description: January 2025 social posts reported mass raids in Pueblo; CPR confirmed the incident involved ICE assisting a narcotics arrest, but fear persisted and door-knock claims spread statewide.
risks.impact: Can trigger unnecessary school/work absences, hamper reporting, and obscure real enforcement actions.
recommended_actions: Verify sightings through CORRN hotline before sharing.
Issue clarifying messages when rumors are debunked.
Maintain rapid logging (time, location, vehicles) for confirmed operations.

risks.title: ICE enforcement quadrupled in Colorado
risks.description: ICE arrests in Colorado nearly quadrupled between January-June 2025 compared to same period in 2024 (1,360 arrests). September 2025 operation targeted immigration fugitives in 14 Colorado cities including Pueblo.
risks.impact: Increased enforcement activity means higher risk for undocumented residents and mixed-status families.
recommended_actions: Program CORRN hotline into all phones.
Prepare family emergency plans and power of attorney documents.
Know location of nearest legal aid (Catholic Charities, RMIAN).

risks.title: Huerfano County ICE detention facility
risks.description: ICE plans to take over Huerfano County Correctional Center in Walsenburg (50 miles south of Pueblo) with 752-person capacity. Community protests at Pueblo City Council over potential ICE use of Pueblo Memorial Airport.
risks.impact: Nearby detention facility increases local ICE activity and transport through Pueblo area.
recommended_actions: Monitor airport and highway for ICE transport vehicles.
Document any ICE activity at Pueblo Memorial Airport.
Support local advocacy against facility activation.

risks.title: ICE 24/7 social media monitoring expansion
risks.description: ICE published RFI for contractors to launch round-the-clock social media monitoring across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Twitter/X, WhatsApp, YouTube, Reddit and more. May expand to monitor friends and relatives of targets.
risks.impact: Digital footprints can be used to identify, locate, and build cases against immigrants and their networks.
recommended_actions: Review social media privacy settings immediately.
Remove location data from posts.
Use Signal for sensitive communications, not WhatsApp.
Warn community about social media surveillance risks.

risks.title: Unlisted ICE hold room serving Pueblo area (PUEHOLD), holds exceeding legal limits
risks.description: FOIA data revealed nine ICE hold rooms in Colorado absent from ICE's public facility list, which names only Aurora. The 'PUEHOLD' room is an ICE substation at 935 State Highway 67 near the Fremont County airport - despite the name it is NOT in the city of Pueblo. It held 315 people across multiple stays Jan-Oct 2025 (statewide: 2,831 across nine rooms; Denver 1,398, Frederick 526). Records showed at least three stays of roughly 12, 14 and 19 days, far past the legal limit, and before a June 2025 memo extended the allowed period from 12 to 72 hours.
risks.impact: Families cannot locate detained relatives because ICE's online locator may not reflect people held in unlisted hold rooms. Absence from the locator is NOT evidence a person is not detained. Prolonged holds occur with little outside oversight.
recommended_actions: Do not treat the ICE online detainee locator as conclusive; ask specifically about hold rooms.
Call RMIAN detention hotline (303) 866-9308 and CORRN 844-864-8341 and ask about hold rooms, not only Aurora.
Document any hold exceeding 72 hours and report to ACLU of Colorado - it is a documentable violation.
Add 'ICE hold room / substation' to the Detention Tracking Template facility field.

risks.title: Courthouse arrest loophole: SB20-83 does not reach federal or combined courthouses
risks.description: SB20-83 bars civil immigration arrests at and immediately outside county, municipal and state courthouses and protects travel to and from court; SB25-276 extended it to related treatment facilities. It does NOT apply to federal courthouses, and advocates report ICE exploiting combined state/federal buildings. CIRC also reports ICE reading court dockets for Spanish and Latin American surnames and detaining people days after a court appearance, away from the courthouse where the statute does not protect them, including people who appeared as crime victims. Documented in Glenwood Springs, Durango/La Plata, Montezuma County and Pagosa Springs; CORRN confirmed SB20-83 violations at Denver's Lindsey-Flannigan Courthouse. No confirmed Pueblo County Courthouse incident in this window, but docket harvesting is not location-specific.
risks.impact: The risk window extends for days after a court date, not just the courthouse visit. Crime victims and witnesses are exposed, which deters reporting.
recommended_actions: Ask counsel about virtual court appearance - CIRC now recommends it.
Request court accompaniment through CIRC.
Confirm whether the courthouse is state-only or a combined state/federal building, because protection differs.
Understand exposure continues for days after the appearance.
Add a 'houses federal proceedings?' field to the Courthouse Monitoring Template.

risks.title: Enforcement pace held at ~12 arrests/day into 2026; 65% had no prior conviction
risks.description: Colorado ICE arrests totaled 4,160 in 2025 vs 1,091 in 2024, a 281% increase (better-sourced than the earlier ~300% estimate). Daily average rose from ~4 to ~12, peaked around April 2025, and HELD at about 12 per day from Jan 1 to Mar 10 2026 - the surge did not recede. 65% of those arrested had no prior criminal conviction; of those with convictions only ~5% involved violent offenses, most commonly DUI, assault and traffic offenses. County data through mid-Oct 2025 put Pueblo County among Colorado's highest-arrest counties after Denver (1,548), El Paso, Arapahoe, Mesa and Adams. Casa de Paz assisted 610 people released from Aurora in 2025 (~40% Colorado residents) vs 2,087 in 2024 (mostly out-of-state arrests), showing a shift toward detaining Colorado residents.
risks.impact: Pueblo County's high ranking plus a sustained statewide pace means local risk is ongoing, not receding. The 65% figure shows enforcement is not limited to people with criminal records, so risk-tiering advice is unsafe.
recommended_actions: Use the 65%-no-conviction figure to justify universal KYR preparation rather than risk-tiering.
Build standing local Pueblo rapid-response capacity rather than relying on Denver-based responders.
Maintain family emergency plans, powers of attorney, and childcare designations regardless of criminal history.

risks.title: Colorado detention capacity nearly doubles: GEO wins 1,200-bed Hudson ICE contract
risks.description: On July 14-15 2026 GEO announced a five-year ICE contract for the 1,200-bed Big Horn Correctional Facility in Hudson (Weld County, ~30 miles NE of Denver), leased from Highlands REIT, projected at ~$85M annual revenue in year one. With Aurora (capacity raised 1,360 to 1,530 in late 2025; FY2026 year-to-date population 1,226), statewide ICE capacity moves to roughly 2,700 beds. Colorado's 2023 ban on state/local ICE detention contracts does not reach privately owned facilities. Senators Hickenlooper and Bennet and Rep. Pettersen opposed the expansion; Bennet announced a blocking strategy May 27 2026 and introduced the KIDS, TRUST and OPEN Acts May 20 2026.
risks.impact: Pueblo-area detainees may be held farther away and transferred more often. Hudson is ~140 miles from Pueblo vs ~120 to Aurora. Transfers routinely break attorney contact. More in-state beds also means more local arrests can be absorbed without out-of-state transfer.
recommended_actions: Add Hudson to every detainee-locating checklist and family visitation plan.
Record the A-number and re-check the ICE locator after any transfer.
Warn families that transfer commonly severs attorney contact - re-establish immediately.

risks.title: Tuberculosis at Aurora ICE facility; GEO obstructing state health investigation
risks.description: Adams County Health Department confirmed an active TB case in a detainee at the Aurora ICE Processing Center around July 14 2026. The Guardian reported an outbreak sickening at least 12 people, unconfirmed by local officials. Colorado officials said GEO Group failed to provide access required under state law for the TB investigation, obstructing contact tracing of exposed people. End-2025 health staffing was one physician, two physician assistants and 18 RNs/NPs for ~1,226 detainees. Aurora is currently the primary destination for detained Pueblo-area residents.
risks.impact: Communicable disease risk for detainees, released people, and their households, with contact tracing blocked.
recommended_actions: Advise anyone released from Aurora in mid-2026 to seek TB screening.
Raise known medical conditions with counsel immediately - medical need supports bond and humanitarian release.
From 2026-08-12, cite HB26-1276 to demand CDPHE inspection records and penalize refused access.
Route Pueblo residents to local low-barrier clinics rather than deferring care.

risks.title: No state limit on ICE reaching local ALPR and location data after 2026 bills died
risks.description: All three 2026 Colorado bills that would have limited government and ICE access to location and broker data failed: SB26-070 (historical location database ban, the 'PEEPS Act') died at adjournment May 13 2026 after being laid over from April 23; SB26-071 (SAFE Act, surveillance technology) was postponed indefinitely 6-1 in Senate Judiciary May 6 2026; HB26-1037 (ban on government purchase of broker data) was postponed indefinitely in House Judiciary April 22 2026. Colorado ALPR data therefore remains governed only by each agency's own policy. ICE has no Flock contract, but the documented national pattern is ICE asking local agencies to run searches for it - local and state police ran immigration-related ALPR searches 4,000+ times between June 2024 and May 2025 across networks covering 5,000+ communities. Flock added a one-toggle federal-sharing shutoff in January 2026 and a state-law disclaimer in February 2026, but both are discretionary agency settings, not legal limits. Boulder disabled national lookup in June 2025 and restricted sharing to in-state agencies, showing agency policy is the only operative control.
risks.impact: Vehicle location histories of Pueblo residents remain accessible to federal immigration enforcement through local agency cooperation, with no state-law backstop and no warrant requirement.
recommended_actions: File records requests with Pueblo PD and PCSO for ALPR audit logs, federal-sharing/national-lookup configuration, and any immigration-related federal search requests received.
Publicly ask both agencies to disable federal sharing, citing Boulder as precedent.
Explain that ALPR captures plates regardless of who is driving, so routine travel patterns are logged.
Re-run this advocacy in the 2027 session since no state protection currently exists.

policies.title: Pueblo County Sheriff cooperation limits (reaffirmed 2026)
policies.summary: Sheriff David Lucero reiterated PCSO will not help ICE with civil 'round-up' operations and will only participate when there are criminal charges or officer-safety concerns. January 2026 interview repeated stance amid statewide arrests.

will_not_cooperate: Enforcement based solely on immigration status
Operations at schools, churches, or similar venues

policies.key_quote: My role isn't to enforce immigration laws. I am not the federal sheriff. My role is to enforce Colorado law and to ensure the safety of the citizens of Pueblo County.
policies.implications: Provides a documented commitment to cite if deputies assist immigration enforcement absent criminal nexus.
actions: Carry copies of the statement at protests, schools, and clinics.
Log any deviations for escalation to POST/AG Pattern & Practice.
sources: Pueblo County Sheriff's Office news release, 2025-01-23

policies.title: Federal court orders ICE to stop warrantless arrests in Colorado
policies.summary: Senior U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued 66-page ruling finding ICE has routinely carried out illegal arrests in Colorado, ordering agents to stop making warrantless arrests based on suspected immigration violations.
policies.implications: Major legal victory limiting ICE tactics in Colorado. Can be cited in any interaction with ICE agents.
actions: Share ruling summary with community members.
Document any warrantless arrests for legal action.
Contact ACLU or RMIAN if witnessing potential violations.

policies.title: Pueblo County Jail ICE detainer policy
policies.summary: PCSO does NOT proactively notify ICE of individuals' immigration status. Follows Colorado state law. Only responded to one ICE inquiry in 2024. ICE must provide warrant or writ signed by federal judge to request hold.

details.fingerprint_process: All booked individuals fingerprinted; FBI sends data to ICE automatically
details.detainer_requirements: ICE must contact jail directly with warrant/writ from federal judge
details.cannot_detain: Cannot hold people after release solely for ICE pickup

policies.title: Pueblo designated 'sanctuary jurisdiction' by DHS
policies.summary: DHS designated Pueblo County as sanctuary jurisdiction in May 2025. List amended within one day, then pulled. August 2025: DOJ listed Colorado as 'sanctuary state' but removed county designations.
policies.local_response: County Commissioners declared Pueblo County is NOT a sanctuary county. Sheriff clarified cooperation within state law bounds.

policies.title: City Council rejected pro-immigrant resolution
policies.summary: Resolution expressing 'support for immigrants' while complying with state law failed 5-2. Would have aligned city policy with Colorado law on immigration detainers.
policies.context: Vote followed protests at City Council over ICE's potential use of Pueblo Memorial Airport.

policies.title: ICE sensitive areas policy rescinded
policies.summary: Acting DHS Secretary rescinded prohibition on ICE arrests in 'sensitive areas' (schools, places of worship, hospitals) on January 21, 2025. ICE can now conduct enforcement at previously protected locations.
policies.implications: Schools, churches, and hospitals are no longer protected from ICE enforcement.
actions: Update community about policy change.
Develop rapid response plans for sensitive locations.
Train staff at schools/churches on KYR protocols.

policies.title: Ramirez Ovando v. Noem - CURRENT STATUS as of 2026-07-29: injunction in effect, on appeal, not stayed
policies.summary: The November 25 2025 preliminary injunction of Senior U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson (D. Colo., No. 1:25-cv-03183-RBJ) barring ICE warrantless arrests in Colorado without a documented individualized flight-risk assessment REMAINS IN FULL EFFECT. The government appealed to the Tenth Circuit on January 23 2026 (No. 26-1027) and filed its opening brief June 1 2026. The appeal is PENDING AND UNDECIDED, NO STAY has been entered, and there is no Supreme Court action. The district court has continued to enforce the injunction: on May 12 2026, after a March 10-11 2026 evidentiary hearing, the court found ICE 'materially violated' both the injunction and federal law. A further motion to enforce remained under advisement as of the July 22 2026 docket update. Plaintiffs' February 3 2026 amended complaint alleges ICE used 'field warrants' issued AFTER an encounter began to circumvent the order, and alleges an internal quota of roughly 75 arrests per day.
policies.confidence: HIGH that the injunction is currently in effect and enforceable; the appeal creates real forward uncertainty, so status is current-but-provisional and must be re-verified before any reprint of Know-Your-Rights material.

details.still_good_law: Yes as of 2026-07-29 - may be cited, but describe as 'on appeal' rather than settled.
remedies_ordered_2026_05_12: ICE must develop compliance training within two weeks.
Every officer authorized to make warrantless arrests in Colorado must be trained within 45 days.
Untrained officers, including new hires, are BARRED from making warrantless arrests until trained.
ICE must produce I-213 forms for warrantless arrests and for arrests on field warrants issued after an encounter began.
ICE must produce arrest lists with A-numbers, country of origin, arrest date and warrant status for plaintiff-counsel review.
details.who_was_affected: Court found affected people included parents of U.S.-citizen children, people with no criminal record, longtime residents, and asylum seekers.

policies.implications: Strongest current documentation tool in Colorado. Observers should record whether any individualized flight-risk assessment appeared to occur and whether a warrant existed BEFORE the encounter began. The court has an active compliance-monitoring channel, so contemporaneous reports carry real leverage.
actions: Cite as 'Ramirez Ovando v. Noem (D. Colo. Nov. 25, 2025), enforced May 12, 2026 - on appeal, 10th Cir. No. 26-1027'.
Check the Tenth Circuit docket monthly; an adverse decision requires same-week correction of every handout.
Report suspected violations to ACLU of Colorado and CORRN 844-864-8341.
Note timestamps: a warrant produced only after an encounter began is the exact pattern the court examined.
sources: Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse, https://clearinghouse.net/case/47063/ (accessed 2026-07-29, docket updated 2026-07-22)

policies.title: Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo (SCOTUS, 2025-09-08) - ethnicity, language and location allowed as stop factors
policies.summary: In a 6-3 emergency-docket order with no full briefing, no oral argument and no majority opinion, the Supreme Court stayed a California district court injunction that had barred ICE 'roving patrol' stops based on apparent ethnicity, speaking Spanish or accented English, presence at a particular location, or type of work. Effect: those factors may be used as part of reasonable suspicion for an immigration stop. Still in force as of July 2026. This ruling was missing from the repo baseline.
policies.confidence: HIGH that the order issued and remains in force; because it was an emergency-docket stay without a majority opinion, its precise doctrinal scope is contested.
policies.implications: Materially changes what KYR material should say. An ICE stop may lawfully be initiated on grounds of appearance or language, so the practical protection is the right to remain silent and to decline consent - NOT an assurance that such a stop is itself unlawful. Pair with Ramirez Ovando, which still constrains warrantless ARREST in Colorado even where a stop is permitted.
actions: Correct any handout implying a stop based on appearance or language is per se unlawful.
Reframe to: 'You do not have to answer questions about where you were born or your immigration status. Say: I want to remain silent. I do not consent to a search.'
Teach the stop/arrest distinction: a permitted stop does not authorize a warrantless arrest without a documented flight-risk finding in Colorado.

policies.title: HB26-1276 SIGNED - detention inspections, PII protections, POST detainer training
policies.summary: 'Protect Safety of Individuals Who Are Immigrants.' Signed by Governor Polis June 4 2026 (Chapter 371, 2026 Session Laws), effective August 12 2026. CDPHE gains expanded authority and increased frequency of inspections of facilities housing noncitizens in civil immigration proceedings, with civil penalties for refusing inspection, an inspection cash fund, and annual public compliance reports to the Attorney General. The Attorney General must develop and publish a policy protecting personal identifying information under Colorado's civil-immigration laws. The POST Board must set peace-officer training standards on current civil immigration detainer law, with certification required by December 31 2027. The court e-filing system is exempted from certain non-disclosure pledge requirements. Appropriation $107,283.
policies.implications: The main affirmative state protection enacted in 2026 and the legal hook for demanding inspection records at any Colorado immigration detention facility, including Walsenburg if it opens.
actions: After 2026-08-12, request CDPHE inspection reports for any facility holding Pueblo-area residents - they must be posted publicly.
Track whether the AG actually publishes the PII policy; that document determines protection against state/local data reaching ICE.
Ask PCSO and Pueblo PD whether officers have completed POST detainer-law training.

policies.title: SB26-005 VETOED - no new state-court remedy against immigration agents
policies.summary: 'Rights Violation in Immigration Enforcement Remedy' would have created a state-court cause of action against anyone acting under color of law in civil immigration enforcement who violated a person's federal constitutional rights, with a two-year limitations period and a $125,604 appropriation to the Department of Law. It passed both chambers on roughly party-line votes in early May 2026 and was VETOED by Governor Polis on June 3 2026. It is NOT law. Correcting the record: secondary trackers described it as 'awaiting signature' as of early June; the primary legislative record shows the veto.
policies.implications: Do not tell community members a new state-court remedy against ICE agents exists. Remedies remain federal (Bivens-limited, plus Ramirez Ovando class relief) and Colorado's existing SB25-276/SB20-83 provisions, which reach state and local employees rather than federal agents.
actions: Remove any reference to a state-court cause of action against federal immigration agents.

Note that SB25-276/SB20-83 enforcement applies to state and local employees only - the AG dropped a suit against a Mesa County deputy once he resigned, because the laws reach only state/local employees.

policies.title: Pueblo City Council Feb 9 2026 agenda: proposed opposition to SB26-070 and SB26-071
policies.summary: The published agenda for Council's third regular meeting of 2026 carried three resolutions on state surveillance legislation: OPPOSE SB26-071 (law enforcement surveillance technology regulation), OPPOSE SB26-070 (historical location database ban), and SUPPORT HB26-1071 (allowing local governments to place automated vehicle identification systems on federal interstate highways). NOTE: HB26-1071 is a DIFFERENT bill from HB26-1037 - do not conflate. Significance: the two bills Council was asked to oppose are precisely those that would have restricted government access to and sharing of vehicle-location data, the pipeline through which ICE most commonly reaches local ALPR data, while the bill Council was asked to support would expand automated vehicle surveillance infrastructure.
policies.confidence: MEDIUM - sourced from the agenda preview. The final recorded vote on each resolution was NOT confirmed. Verify against official Council minutes before asserting Council 'voted to oppose.'
policies.implications: If adopted, the city actively lobbied against state limits on ICE access to local location data while Pueblo County ranks among Colorado's highest ICE-arrest counties.
actions: Pull the official Feb 9 2026 Council minutes to confirm the votes.
Raise at public comment: opposition to SB26-070/071 leaves residents' location data governed only by department policy.
Ask Council to pair AVIS expansion support with a binding local policy barring federal immigration data sharing.
sources: Colorado Municipal League position paper on SB26-071, https://www.cml.org/home/publications-news/resource-detail/position-paper-sb26-71-use-of-surveillance-technology-by-law-enforcement

policies.title: Walsenburg / Huerfano County facility - NOT open as ICE detention as of 2026-07-29
policies.summary: As of July 29 2026 the Walsenburg facility has NOT opened as an ICE detention center and no ICE-CoreCivic contract has been announced. Governor Polis proposed the state buy it for roughly $150-200 million to relieve prison crowding; the legislature's Joint Budget Committee REJECTED that purchase on March 31 2026 citing a $1.5 billion state shortfall, reviving fears of an ICE deal. On CoreCivic's May 7 2026 Q1 earnings call there was no indication an ICE contract for Huerfano was imminent, though leadership expressed general optimism for the second half of 2026. Opponents organized as Speak Up SOCO filed a municipal ballot initiative April 9 2026 to amend Walsenburg zoning to prohibit immigrant detention at the site, set for the November 3 2026 ballot. At the July 7 2026 Walsenburg City Council meeting advocates urged direct adoption of the ordinance, fearing a deal could close before the election.
policies.capacity_note: Figures conflict across sources: 752 beds (built capacity, most commonly cited in 2025-2026 reporting), ~700 (state purchase discussions), and 1,400 (2025 ICE planning documents, likely double-bunked). Treat 752 as the base figure and 1,400 as a maximum-density planning number. The repo previously carried both 1,400 and 752.
policies.implications: Closest large-scale detention risk to Pueblo (~50 miles). Status could change on any contract announcement, and the gap between announcement and first intake would be short.
actions: Keep as a live monitoring item; re-check before each community meeting.
Pre-build now: RMIAN intake protocol, visitation transport plan, Pueblo-to-Walsenburg travel logistics.
Coordinate with Speak Up SOCO for regional solidarity ahead of the Nov 3 2026 vote.
If it opens after 2026-08-12, immediately demand CDPHE inspection reports under HB26-1276.

policies.title: PCSO / Pueblo PD cooperation posture - no documented change since January 2026
policies.summary: No evidence of any change to PCSO's stated posture since the January 2026 restatement: no participation in ICE roundups or sweeps, cooperation only where there are criminal charges or a criminal nexus, or officer-safety backup. NO 287(g) agreement was found for Pueblo County or Pueblo PD in this research window; Colorado law restricts such agreements and nothing indicates Pueblo entered one. Existing jail practice stands: everyone booked is fingerprinted and the FBI transmits data to ICE automatically, so a criminal booking remains the main pathway to ICE contact regardless of the Sheriff's stance; ICE must present a warrant or writ signed by a federal judge; the jail cannot hold someone past release solely for ICE pickup.
policies.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH on the sheriff's posture and absence of 287(g). LOW on ALPR: no Pueblo-specific record was found of PD or PCSO plate data flowing to ICE, and no source confirms whether federal sharing is enabled. This is an unverified gap, NOT a clean bill of health.
open_items: A February 12 2026 Pueblo County Commissioners resolution touching immigration designation was referenced in local coverage, but its text and effect COULD NOT BE VERIFIED. Obtain from the Clerk to the Board before characterizing the county's position.
Board of County Commissioners TABLED competing 'non-sanctuary' resolutions June 10 2025 after extended public comment; neither was adopted.
Pueblo City Council rejected a pro-immigrant resolution 5-2 on November 10 2025.
actions: Request PCSO monthly ICE detainer and ICE-inquiry counts for 2026 to test stated policy against practice.
Request Pueblo PD and PCSO ALPR audit logs and federal-sharing configuration.
Obtain the Feb 12 2026 commissioners' resolution text: https://county.pueblo.org/board-county-commissioners/resolutions-minutes-and-agendas
Keep citing the Sheriff's statement at schools and clinics, while being clear it does NOT stop the fingerprint-to-ICE pipeline after a booking.
